title: Electric shock — cut the power before you touch them
applies_to: Someone who has touched live electricity: a socket, a bare wire, a machine, or a fallen power line.

citations.source: WHO and IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2020
European Resuscitation Council Guidelines 2021: Special Circumstances

steps.text: Look before you touch anything. If they are still in contact with the electricity, they are live, and so is anything touching them.
Switch the power off at the fuse box, or pull the plug out. That is safer and faster than pulling at the person.
If you cannot switch it off, stand on something dry and push them clear with something dry that does not carry current, such as a wooden broom.
Call for an ambulance. Say it was an electric shock, and say whether it was a house socket or a power line.
Once they are clear, tap their shoulders and shout. Look at the chest for up to 10 seconds.
If the chest is not rising and falling normally, lay them flat and press hard and fast on the middle of the chest. Keep going.
If they are breathing, keep them lying still and look for burns where the current went in and where it came out.
Cool any burn under cool running water and cover it loosely with a clean dry cloth.
They must be checked at a hospital even if they now feel fine. Electricity can upset the heart hours later.

do_not: Do not touch them while they are still in contact with the electricity.
Do not go near a fallen power line. Stay at least 10 metres back and wait for the power company.
Do not use anything wet, or anything made of metal, to push them clear.
Do not let them go home to rest without being seen.
Do not stand in water while you work on this.
escalate_if: It was a high voltage line, or lightning — treat it as an emergency even if they look well.
They stop answering you and stop breathing normally — start pushing on the chest.
They say their heart is racing or skipping — say this on the phone.
They were thrown or fell — a bone may be broken and the neck may be hurt.
The burn goes deeper than it looks, or the limb is going numb — tell the crew.
